title: From Block-encoding to Generalized Quantum Signal Processing: Principles, Algorithms and Applications
authors: Tal Gurfinkel, Kaushika De Silva, Anuradha Mahasinghe, Jens Renders, Jack Blyth, James Greenwell, Archie Butterworth, Yusen Wu, Lyle Noakes, Miloud Bessafi, Frederic Cadet, Jingbo Wang
abstract: Modern quantum algorithms are increasingly formulated as coherent procedures for implementing polynomial transformations of operators and singular values. This perspective provides a powerful and unifying language for quantum algorithm design, connecting a wide range of distinct problems through five closely related key tools: block-encoding, qubitization, QSP, QSVT and GQSP. Block-encoding embeds non-unitary matrices into larger unitaries; qubitization converts block-encodings into structured operators; QSP, QSVT and GQSP enable polynomial transformations with near-optimal query complexity. Together, these techniques form a general toolkit for transforming matrix functions into implementable quantum circuits. This paper develops these techniques from first principles as a unified framework for constructing quantum algorithms. We apply this framework to representative applications to highlight design principles and demonstrate how distinct algorithms can be constructed from a unified sequence of operator transformations.   A central contribution is a systematic decision workflow for selecting the appropriate approach according to the operator structure and the desired transformation polynomial. This perspective clarifies when direct GQSP or through qubitization, or Laurent expansion, or QSVT is most appropriate. We organize algorithmic design into an end-to-end pipeline: identifying the target matrix function, constructing an appropriate block-encoding, determining the relevant spectral domain, designing a polynomial or Laurent-polynomial approximation, synthesizing the phase factors, and translating the transformation into an executable quantum circuit. By applying this unified framework to example applications, we showcase a practical methodology for reasoning, designing, and implementing quantum algorithms based on polynomial transformations.
summary: This paper presents a unified theoretical framework for designing quantum algorithms to compute functions of matrices. It systematically connects several key techniques—including block-encoding, QSP, and QSVT—into a single pipeline. This allows researchers to choose the optimal method for implementing complex linear algebra tasks on quantum hardware.
main_problem: The core problem is implementing complex, often non-unitary, matrix functions (like inverses or matrix exponentials) using quantum computation, which is fundamentally unitary.
main_result: The paper develops a unified, systematic framework connecting block-encoding, qubitization, QSP, QSVT, and GQSP to construct quantum circuits for arbitrary operator transformations.
method: The methodology involves an end-to-end pipeline: identifying the target function, constructing a block-encoding, determining the spectral domain, approximating the function with a polynomial, and synthesizing the final quantum circuit.
model_or_system: The model is general quantum computation applied to linear algebra problems, focusing on transforming operators and singular values rather than simulating specific physical Hamiltonians.
key_observables: Success probability of block-encoding, absolute errors of polynomial approximations, and the spectral information encoded in eigenphases.
important_parameters: The choice between GQSP, QSVT, or qubitization depends on the operator structure and the desired polynomial approximation.
main_assumptions: The framework relies on the ability to construct efficient block-encodings and the assumption that polynomial approximations can achieve sufficient accuracy for the target function.
figures_summary: Figures compare polynomial approximations (Chebyshev vs. power-basis) to exact functions and show comparisons of solutions for financial problems (Black-Scholes) using various numerical and quantum methods.
paper_structure: The paper builds from foundational tools (block-encoding, QSP) to advanced generalizations (QSVT, GQSP), culminating in a systematic decision workflow that guides the design of quantum algorithms for matrix functions.
why_interesting: While highly algorithmic, the focus on general operator transformations and spectral methods provides a powerful mathematical toolkit that underpins many quantum simulation techniques relevant to AMO physics.
